item.title: Coal power lives longer next to data centres
item.content:encoded:
Nature Climate Change, Published online: 10 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41558-026-02769-9

Data centres are among the world’s fastest growing electricity consumers. An analysis of more than 9,000 facilities worldwide links the artificial intelligence-era expansion of data centres to delayed coal plant retirements and around 2 Gt of additional carbon dioxide emissions.
item.dc:title: Coal power lives longer next to data centres
item.dc:creator: Anton Pichler

item.title: Higher warming leads to a larger zero-emissions commitment
item.content:encoded:
Nature Climate Change, Published online: 10 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41558-026-02789-5

Scientific grounds for a net-zero policy assume near-zero committed warming over a few decades after CO2 emissions cease. A modelling study suggests that if prior peak temperatures rise above 2 °C before cessation of CO2 emissions, committed warming increases, making it harder to stabilize global warming.
item.dc:title: Higher warming leads to a larger zero-emissions commitment
item.dc:creator: June-Yi Lee

item.title: Early evidence links data centre exposure to coal power retirement timelines
item.content:encoded:
Nature Climate Change, Published online: 10 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41558-026-02794-8

Data centre expansion may slow the coal-fired power plants phase-out, complicating decarbonization pathways. This study finds that coal units exposed to post-2020 data centres have lower retirement risks and their potential lifetime extensions could cause large additional CO2 emissions.
item.dc:title: Early evidence links data centre exposure to coal power retirement timelines
